records.place: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch ward, Stellenbosch district, Western Cape

wine.name: Kanonkop Paul Sauer
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, traditionally about seven tenths, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot in roughly equal parts for the rest; the shares move with the year.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards on the lower slopes of the Simonsberg, in decomposed granite with Hutton and Clovelly soils, trellised and farmed for small crops.
wine.making: Fermented in open concrete fermenters, the cap of skins punched down by hand every two hours through the ferment, as the house describes it. The wine then matures for about two years in new French oak barriques, Nevers oak in the house's recent notes, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Cassis, plum and sour cherry over cedar, cigar box and tobacco leaf; full and firm, with a dense, fine tannin that takes years to soften and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Closed for much of its first decade in a strong vintage; the house gives it twenty to twenty five years, and longer in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the blend, honouring the cabinet minister who owned the farm and died in 1976.
The ward on the Simonsberg's lower slopes within the Stellenbosch district; every grape must have grown in it.
The Cape's certification of origin, vintage and variety, shown by a numbered seal on the bottle's neck.

records.table: Kanonkop is the Simonsberg estate whose Paul Sauer, first made in 1981, is a Cabernet led Bordeaux blend named for the cabinet minister who owned the farm. Fermented in open concrete tanks and aged two years in new French oak, it is firm and cedary, so decant it.
records.story: The name, as the house tells it, comes from a hillock on the Simonsberg above the farm, where in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a cannon was fired to announce sailing ships entering Table Bay. After the First World War the farm passed to Paul Sauer (1898 to 1976), son of a Cape cabinet minister and himself a minister in the National Party governments from 1948 into the 1960s. In 1973 his son-in-law and the estate's winemaker bottled the first wines under the Kanonkop label, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage among them; Sauer, by the house's account, was uneasy at first, for he had close ties to the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery. He died in 1976, and the farm passed to his daughter and her husband, the Krige family. With the 1981 vintage the estate made its first Bordeaux blend and gave it his name: Paul Sauer, Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Merlot, fermented in open concrete tanks with the cap punched down by hand and aged in new French oak. Kanonkop is known above all for Pinotage, yet Paul Sauer holds none, so it is no Cape Blend. For a sommelier it is the Stellenbosch Cabernet blend to name first, and the proof that Kanonkop is more than its Pinotage.

Paul Sauer the wine was first made in 1981, five years after the death of Paul Sauer the man in 1976.

report: The estate's domain refused a fetch, so its pages were read through search summaries: they give 1919 as the year Paul Sauer took the farm, while two secondary accounts give 1929, so founded is empty and the story says after the First World War.
Wikipedia says he inherited the farm from his father, Jacobus Wilhelmus Sauer, who died in 1913; the house calls him its first owner, and the record says only that the farm passed to him.
The first Paul Sauer of 1981 rests on the house, the library (w-paul-sauer) and secondary accounts; the 1973 first bottling on the house and two secondary accounts.
The ward on the label rests on the house's factsheets (origin Simonsberg, Stellenbosch), one review and the library's sub-region; the exact wording of the front label was not seen.
The cannon story is the house's own and is told as such; the dates of the cannon differ between sources (seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the house's words), so the record keeps the house's.
The living owners, the winemakers of 1973, 1981 and since, and Sauer's daughter and son-in-law are described, never named.
No swap proposed.

records.place: Southern Stellenbosch near False Bay, Stellenbosch district, Western Cape

wine.name: Meerlust Rubicon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, most often about two thirds, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc and, in vintages since the late 2000s, a little Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards in the cool south of Stellenbosch near False Bay: weathered granite on the warm Compagniesdrift hill, clay of an old estuary on the lowlands, shale at the Quarry, sand and river stones on the terraces.
wine.making: Each variety is fermented apart, with pump overs and délestage, and goes through malolactic fermentation in barrel. After some months the components are blended and returned to French oak, mostly Nevers and more than half of it new, for sixteen to twenty one months in all; the wine then rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Violet, ripe plum, blackberry and cassis over cedar, fennel and liquorice; restrained rather than heavy, with fine, firm tannin and a dry finish that turns to cigar box and tobacco leaf with age.
wine.ageing: Opens after some years in bottle and develops for ten to twenty years by the house's estimate, longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the blend: crossing the Rubicon, a step with no turning back.
The district named under Wine of Origin; every grape in the bottle grew within it.
The Cape's scheme of 1973 that certifies origin, vintage and variety, sealed on the bottle's neck.

records.table: Meerlust is the False Bay estate the Myburgh family bought in 1756, and Rubicon, first made in 1980, is its Cabernet led Bordeaux blend with Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Violet, plum and cedar come with restraint rather than weight, and it rewards years in bottle.
records.story: A German settler took up the farm in 1693, as the estate tells it, and named it Meerlust, roughly the pleasure of the sea, for the view from its granite outcrop five kilometres from False Bay. In 1756 the Myburgh family bought it, eight generations by their own count. The homestead's front gable marks 1776, the year its extension was completed, and the whole farmstead has been declared a national monument. For more than two centuries Meerlust sold its grapes and wine in bulk; the seventh generation of the family turned it towards bottling under the estate's own name, beginning with a Cabernet Sauvignon in the 1970s. Drawn to Bordeaux, he and his winemaker set out to blend Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the Médoc manner, and the 1980 vintage became Rubicon, among the first Bordeaux blends of the modern Cape. A poet friend at the University of Stellenbosch suggested the name, as the family tells it: like crossing the Rubicon, the decision could not be undone. At his death in 1988 his son, the eighth generation, took over. For a sommelier Rubicon is where the Cape's Bordeaux blend begins, and a wine made to be kept.

report: The plan's why says the Myburgh family has held Meerlust since 1757; the estate's own pages, a secondary account and the library (p-meerlust) say 1756, which the record follows, so the why should read 1756.
The release of the 1980 Rubicon is dated 1983 in one account and 1984 in another (the estate's milestones), so the record gives only the vintage.
Trial blends from 1978 and a Bordeaux journey of 1967 rest on one secondary source each and are left out.

The seventh generation (Nico Myburgh, who died in 1988) and the poet who named the wine are described, not named, since their dates were not found in two sources; the winemaker of 1980 and the eighth generation are living.
The library calls Rubicon South Africa's first Bordeaux style blend; the record says among the first, as the plan does, since no second source settles a first.
The new oak share (55 to 70 per cent) and the time in barrel (16 to 21 months) are read from the house's sheets for 2008 to 2017; later sheets were not read for those figures.
No swap proposed.

wine.name: Rustenberg John X Merriman
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, the two leading in shares that shift with the year, with smaller parts of Petit Verdot and Malbec and, in some years, Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: Only the estate's own vineyards, in decomposed granite on the slopes of the Simonsberg above Stellenbosch.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks with about a week of extended maceration on the skins. The wine is then aged for about twenty months in French oak barriques, around a third of them new and the rest second and third fill, before bottling.
wine.glass: Cassis and blackcurrant with sour cherry and cigar tobacco over fine grained tannin; with age the tannin softens and the palate turns rounder and more savoury.
wine.ageing: Worth decanting in its youth; the house gives it ten to fifteen years from the vintage in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The blend's name, after the Cape prime minister who farmed Schoongezicht, the other half of the estate, from 1892.
The ward on the lower slopes of the Simonsberg, within the Stellenbosch district.
The estate's name, from the farm granted in 1682 and divided in 1810.

records.table: Rustenberg is the Simonsberg estate on a grant of 1682, and John X Merriman is its Bordeaux blend, named for the Cape prime minister who farmed Schoongezicht from 1892. Cabernet and Merlot from decomposed granite give cassis, sour cherry and cigar tobacco.
records.story: The farm goes back to 1682, when, as the estate tells it, a German settler from near the Rhine was granted the land. In 1810 an owner divided it into two farms, Rustenberg and Schoongezicht. Phylloxera struck the Cape's vineyards in the late nineteenth century, and in 1892 John X Merriman (1841 to 1926), the English born politician who would be the last prime minister of the Cape Colony, from 1908 to 1910, took on Schoongezicht, while his brother-in-law took Rustenberg; together they replanted on resistant rootstock. Wine has been bottled at the estate without a break since 1892, by its own account. In 1941 a member of the Barlow family, on leave from his army unit in the Second World War, bought Rustenberg, and in 1945 he added Schoongezicht, joining the two farms again after more than a century apart. The estate's Bordeaux blend carries Merriman's name and draws only on its own vineyards; beside it the single vineyard Peter Barlow Cabernet honours the buyer of 1941. For a sommelier, John X Merriman ties a Simonsberg red to a Cape prime minister, and to an estate that has bottled its own wine for well over a century.

Merriman farmed Schoongezicht, the other half of the divided farm; in 1892 Rustenberg went to his brother-in-law.

report: Rustenberg is not in the library, so its own dates rest on the estate's history page, read through search, with The Wine Society's page on the 2022 John X Merriman agreeing on the division of 1810, the purchases of 1892 and the Barlows' arrival in the 1940s; Merriman's dates and premiership rest on Wikipedia and Britannica, with South African History Online agreeing.
The first vintage of John X Merriman under that name was not found in any source (the earliest factsheet seen is the 2005), so the story gives no first year.

The estate names the grantee of 1682, the owner who divided the farm in 1810, the brother-in-law of 1892 (Sir Jacob Barry on one page, John Barry on another) and the buyer of 1941; none had dates in two sources, so each is described rather than named, the last only through the wine that bears his name.
The first vintage of Peter Barlow, 1996, rests on one retailer listing and is left out.
The phylloxera replanting of 1892 rests on the estate and a secondary account that Merriman bought the farm in sympathy with growers hit by phylloxera.
No swap proposed.

wine.name: Simonsig Kaapse Vonkel Brut
wine.appellation: Stellenbosch or Western Cape, by vintage
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in roughly equal parts, with a little Pinot Meunier; the first vintage, of 1971, was Chenin Blanc.
wine.sites: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Stellenbosch, and in the vintages labelled Western Cape from vineyards beyond the district as well.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in stainless steel at a cool 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, part of the Chardonnay in older French oak barrels, and malolactic fermentation is avoided to keep it fresh. The second fermentation takes place in the bottle, and the wine rests at least twenty months on its lees before disgorging.
wine.glass: Green apple and ripe pear with shortbread from the lees, a fine, lively mousse, fresh, crisp acidity and a delicate, dry finish with a stony edge.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk on release, while its fruit is fresh; kept a few years more it softens and gains toasty depth.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip shaped white wine glass shows it better than a narrow flute.

label.means: Afrikaans for Cape sparkle, the name given to the estate's first sparkling wine.
South Africa's name for sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in the bottle, as in Champagne.
The dry style, as on Champagne labels: little sugar is added at disgorging.
At least 85 per cent of the wine comes from the harvest of that year.

records.table: Simonsig's Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle in Afrikaans, was the first South African sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in the bottle, from the 1971 harvest. First made from Chenin Blanc, it has since moved to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, aged at least twenty months on its lees.
records.story: Simonsig's founder began to farm in 1953, as the family tells it, on De Hoop, a farm he rented from his father-in-law, and in 1964 he bought land of his own. In 1968 he bottled the first wine under the Simonsig name, a Chenin Blanc labelled Steen. A visit to Champagne led him to try its method at home: from the 1971 harvest, with rudimentary equipment and riddling racks he built himself, he made a sparkling wine fermented a second time in its bottle. The Cape grew little Chardonnay or Pinot Noir then, so the wine was Chenin Blanc. He called it Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle, and released it in 1973, the first South African wine of its kind. In 1971, too, by the house's account, Simonsig joined Spier and Delheim in founding the Stellenbosch Wine Route. The blend later moved to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with a little Pinot Meunier beside them. As other cellars took up the method, the Cape's makers formed an association in 1992 and gave the style the name Méthode Cap Classique. For a sommelier, Kaapse Vonkel is where Cap Classique begins: the Cape's own name for the traditional method, and the bottle that started it.

report: The house's own pages say Kaapse Vonkel was released in 1971; the Cap Classique producers' fiftieth anniversary page and the Codex's Cap Classique record say made from the 1971 harvest and released in 1973, which the record follows.

The region record's producers line calls Simonsig the Simonsberg estate and the Codex's Cap Classique record says the wine was made on the Simonsberg; the sources read disagree on where the estate stands against the mountain, so place says only the district.
The founder's dates were not found in two sources (the house says he died in 2003, and no source read gives his birth year), so he is described, not named; his son and grandson are living.
The move to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay is dated 1987, and credited to the founder's son, in one source only, so the story gives neither.
Founded is empty: the family dates its start to 1953 on a rented farm, the purchase of its own land to 1964 and the first Simonsig label to 1968.
The appellation changes by vintage: the house's notes show Wine of Origin Western Cape for 2020 and 2022 and Stellenbosch for 2021 and the 2023 magnum.
The association's founding year, 1992, is the association's own; another account says the founder's son began the group in 1988.
No swap proposed.

records.place: Jonkershoek Valley ward, Stellenbosch district, Western Cape

wine.name: Lanzerac Pinotage
wine.grapes: Pinotage alone, the Cape's own crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, made at Stellenbosch in 1925.
wine.sites: Several blocks of the estate's own vines in the Jonkershoek Valley on the edge of Stellenbosch town, where mountain soils and a mountain climate keep structure and natural acidity in the grapes.
wine.making: Fermented in open wooden fermenters or in stainless steel, by vintage, with regular pump overs; malolactic fermentation follows in barrel, and the wine matures for fifteen months or more in French oak, a share of it new and the rest second and third fill.
wine.glass: Ripe plum and red and black berries with a hint of sweet oak; a rounded, generous mouthfeel, soft tannin and a lingering finish, with chocolate and caramel as it ages.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release; the house gives it five to ten years, in which it gains notes of chocolate and caramel.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle, though an hour of air does no harm; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The Cape's own grape, Pinot Noir crossed with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, in 1925.
The estate's name since 1920, when a new owner renamed the farm once called Schoongezicht.
The district named on the label, home of the estate and of the university where Pinotage was bred.

records.table: Lanzerac is the Jonkershoek Valley estate whose name was on the first label to say Pinotage, the 1959 vintage sold in 1961. Its Lanzerac Pinotage, from its own valley vineyards and matured in French oak, gives ripe plum and berries with a soft, rounded finish.
records.story: Lanzerac dates itself to 1692, when, as the estate tells it, a settler took the land, named the farm Schoongezicht and planted its first vines. In 1920 a new owner bought the farm and renamed it Lanzerac; the story goes that the name honours a French general of the First World War, a tale told rather than recorded. In 1925, at the university in Stellenbosch, Abraham Perold (1880 to 1941), its first professor of viticulture, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, and gave the Cape its own grape. The first wine sold as Pinotage came from the 1959 vintage, from grapes grown and made at the Bellevue farm, by most accounts. It was judged the champion of the young wine show that year, and the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under its Lanzerac label, as the Pinotage Association tells it. The estate counts that label as its own heritage, and its Lanzerac Pinotage, from its own Jonkershoek vineyards, carries the name forward. For a sommelier the lesson is in the detail: the first Pinotage label said Lanzerac, but by most accounts the grapes grew at Bellevue.

others.name: Lanzerac Pionier Pinotage
others.note: The estate's single vineyard Pinotage from a Jonkershoek block planted in 1996, aged up to twenty two months in barriques.

traps: The first wine labelled Pinotage, the 1959 vintage released in 1961, was made by most accounts from Bellevue's grapes and sold under the Lanzerac label of the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery.
Pinotage was crossed in 1925 from Pinot Noir and Cinsaut; Hermitage was the old Cape name for Cinsaut, not Syrah.
The 1959 is the vintage of the first Pinotage label; 1961 is the year it reached the market.

cards.back: Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, then called Hermitage at the Cape, crossed by Abraham Perold in 1925.

Bush vines bought from Swartland growers

Old vines on the Bellevue farm

questions.q: The first wine to name Pinotage on its label came from the 1959 vintage. In which year did it reach the market?
questions.exp: The Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under the Lanzerac label; 1925 is the year of the crossing and 1941 that of the first barrel of Pinotage, made at Elsenburg.

sources.title: Pinotage Association: The Father of Pinotage
Bellevue Estate: 1959, the year Bellevue Pinotage made history

report: Swap proposed, to Vergelegen (its V or GVB Red) or Warwick (Trilogy): the Pinotage Association and Bellevue's own page tell it that the first Pinotage of 1959 was grown and made at Bellevue and released in 1961 by the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery under its Lanzerac label, so the estate's claim is to a merchant's label rather than its own vineyard, and the plan's why overstates it.
Lanzerac is better known as a hotel than as a wine house, Kanonkop already carries Pinotage for the group, and the region record itself names Vergelegen among the houses to name.

The Codex's region summary and producers line say Lanzerac sold the 1959 Pinotage in 1961; the record follows the Pinotage Association, that it was the merchant's Lanzerac label with Bellevue's grapes, hedged as most accounts because one account says the 1959 also held fruit from Kanonkop.
Founded is empty: the estate dates itself to 1692, and a Stellenbosch heritage survey (stellenboschheritage.co.za, Lanzerac historical property) dates the first grant to 1683.

The year of the purchase and renaming is 1920 in the estate's pages and the heritage survey, 1922 in one other account; the survey links the name to a French village, the estate to a rumour of General Lanrezac, so the story keeps the estate's rumour; the survey's reason for the renaming and the hotel of the late 1950s rest on one source each and are left out.
The first grantee and the owner of 1920 are described, not named, since their dates were not found in two sources.
The fermentation vessel differs by vintage in the house's notes (open wooden fermenters, stainless steel), so making says so; the 1996 planting of the Pionier block is the house's own account.
